analysis.one_liner: Requires trucks and trailers to carry rear, side, and front guards that stop cars from sliding underneath in crashes.
analysis.headline: With 13 cosponsors from both parties, the bill sat in the Senate Commerce Committee for 22 months, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill directed the Department of Transportation to require rear, side, and front underride guards on large trucks and trailers, so that a car that collides with one cannot slide underneath and have its passenger compartment crushed. It set crash-test performance standards at 35 mph, required retrofitting older trailers, mandated pre-trip inspections of the guards, created an advisory committee including crash victims' families, and required public reporting of underride crash deaths. It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who rides in a passenger car near large trucks. The bill's stated purpose was to reduce the hundreds of preventable deaths and life-threatening injuries from underride crashes that NHTSA and the NTSB have identified, and it listed dozens of named victims in its findings [S2] [S3]. Drivers and carriers also got a clear inspection checklist for guard integrity [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires rear and side guards strong enough to prevent a passenger compartment intrusion in a 35 mph crash, including off-center impacts covering 50% and 30% of the car's width [S2] [S3].
Extends protection beyond new trailers: requires retrofit rules for trailers and single-unit trucks manufactured before the rules take effect, with phase-in periods of up to 2-3 years [S3].
Requires drivers to inspect underride guards before trips for rust, cracked welds, fractures, and loose fasteners, and to complete repairs before operating the vehicle [S2] [S3].

Creates a Committee on Underride Protection with crash-victim family members, safety engineers, and emergency responders to oversee the rulemaking, and requires DOT to publish quarterly data on underride crash victims [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Truck and trailer manufacturers, which would have to design, certify, and install new guard systems on every qualifying vehicle; motor carriers and trailer owners, which would bear retrofit and inspection costs. Those costs would partly flow through to shipping prices paid by businesses and consumers, in exchange for fewer crash deaths.

drawbacks.text: The retrofit mandate reaches trailers and single-unit trucks already on the road, not just new ones, so the equipment cost falls on the existing fleet immediately, though the Secretary could allow phase-in periods of up to 2-3 years [S3].

The bill fixes the 35 mph performance standard in statute rather than leaving it to agency safety experts, which limits DOT's ability to adjust testing requirements if engineering evidence supports a different standard [S2] [S3].

Adding side and front guards to tens of thousands of trailers imposes per-unit costs on an industry that operates on thin margins, and those costs would be passed into freight prices; the bill offered no funding to offset them [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety upside is large and well documented: federal investigators had already recommended exactly these guards, and the bill memorializes dozens of named victims. The costs are real but bounded — engineering a guard is a one-time per-vehicle cost, and the bill allowed multi-year phase-ins for the existing fleet. The main design criticism is that Congress wrote the crash-test standard into law instead of letting safety experts set it. On balance this is a conventional, well-supported safety mandate whose costs are small next to the deaths it targets.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on day one — and that is the last thing that ever happened to it; the committee never held a hearing or voted, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Gillibrand introduced the bill with nine original cosponsors including Republican Sen. Marco Rubio on March 5, 2019 [S1] [S3].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S1] [S5].
That referral was the bill's final action: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote in the remaining 22 months of the Congress [S1] [S5].

The bill's findings cited NHTSA reporting hundreds of preventable underride deaths and NTSB recommendations for exactly these guards, and it listed named victims including members of the Karth family [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Truck and trailer manufacturers and motor carriers are better off because the bill died: they never faced the guard, retrofit, and inspection mandates. Passenger-vehicle occupants got no new protection, and DOT was left without the committee, reporting, and data requirements.

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors from both parties.

for.name: Sen. Marco Rubio
for.what_they_did: Signed on as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

for.name: 13 senators
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Blumenthal, Markey, Duckworth, Peters, Wyden, Udall, and Feinstein.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and never reported it out — no hearing, no markup, no vote in the 22 months before the Congress ended.

against.name: Trucking and trailer manufacturing industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory side and front underride guard requirements on cost grounds during the period this bill and its successors were debated.

sides.party_line_note: The 13 cosponsors split 11 Democrats, 1 Republican, and 1 Independent, so sponsorship crossed party lines; there were no votes to break down because the bill never left committee.

industries.note: The bill would have required rear, side, and front underride guards meeting a 35 mph crash-test standard on nearly all trailers over 10,000 lbs and on high-clearance single-unit trucks, including retrofits for the existing fleet. Compliance costs are significant, but the guards exist precisely to prevent deaths of car occupants.

Carriers would have absorbed retrofit costs and new pre-trip inspection and repair obligations for underride protection systems, costs that pass into freight prices. The safety benefit accrues to people in the other vehicles involved in collisions.

Fewer catastrophic underride crashes would reduce large bodily-injury claims; one insurer representative would have sat on the advisory committee. Any premium effect would likely be small relative to claims avoided.
